commit.message:
echo: Fix up displayed time and tone values

The echo effect did actually calculate the right values for the sound,
but in the conversion to the metadata model, the "display in right
units" code for these two pots got lost.

The math was done in two places (in echo_time/tone_display() and in
echo_init()) and the 'display' part was lost in the chaos of rewriting
the pot descriptors and re-doing how the effects were defined.

This reinstates the display by teaching the metadata about the special
exponential function that these two pots used, and updating the pot
description to match the match that the effects used to do in two
separate places.

My bad for not noticing immediately - this is all Ricky's code, so I
didn't react to the largely automated conversion.  And that's despite
the fact that I had done the special display conversion in the original
Hothouse conversion case.

So I only noticed that the display code got dropped as part of testing
out the Web UI, and noticing that the numbers looked all kinds of odd
("That 0.5 ms echo time can't be right..  D'oh!")

I think they are back to the real values now.  The Web UI is still a bit
odd with all the excessive precision ("6412.53 Hz" - it really shouldn't
be shown to six significant digits), but at least it looks like the
values are in the right ballpark now.

Fixes: 9c208692f7f1 ("Convert effects to metadata-driven boiler plate generation")
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

WebMIDI: Add toy graphical EQ visualization

This is not the frequency-accurate graph that the pedal screen has, it's
more of a toy-like visual approximation of the sliders, but it's cute.

At least it's cute in my desktop view..  It might be a bit cramped on a
phone screen.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Cache 24c02 eeprom contents, write to it more carefully

The 24c02 eeprom isn't the fanciest of chips, and when it is busy
writing it falls off the i2c bus - and the write can take up to 5ms.

That really wasn't an issue when we only wrote back the effect state
when switching effects manually.  The writes were naturally limited by
the UI update speed.

But the new WebMIDI interface with the "save all effects" option means
that suddenly writes weren't limited by the UI update speed at all, and
they started failing.

The most straightforward solution to this is to just cache the whole
(little) eeprom state in RAM, and have a "eeprom_task()" that writes
back dirty data with the required 5ms delays.  In fact, to keep things
simple, we'll just keep it to the same UI update limit it used to have.

So now loading the effect just reads it from the RAM cache, and saving
the effect just writes it back to the RAM cache and marks it dirty for
later writeback.

In fact, since we buffer it anyway, let's just make the writes be
limited to 8 bytes at a time, so that if I were to ever make the mistake
of getting an older version of the 24c02, it will still work.

The chips I have all have a 16-byte page size, but some old versions
apparently have 8-byte pages and writing 16 bytes at a time wouldn't
work (the second half would just overwrite the first half).

Reading the 24c02 doesn't have any of those issues, and you can just
slurp in the whole 256-byte thing in one go at boot time.

This seems to fix all the saving problems that the new WebMIDI code
exposed.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Make it easier to update the WebMIDI app

Doing the load/save/reset changes made it obvious that the PWA app also
needs to be easy to update, since the app and the pedal are pretty
closely intertwined.

Some day maybe the MIDI CC details are more stable, and we could even
have a discovery protocol, and the tight integration between pedal
firmware and app can be a thing of the past.

But that day isn't today.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add support for effect load/save and reset-to-defaults

Playing around with the WebMIDI interface - that seems to work quite
well - I was easily able to make a mess, particularly with the 10-band
EQ that doesn't have a very nice interface yet.

So I wanted a "reset to defaults" to undo my mess.  But also a load and
save operation to load things to the internal eeprom, or save any
possibly good settings.

All of this either per-effect, or globally for the whole pedal.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Convert effects to metadata-driven boiler plate generation

This is the actual effect format update mentioned in the previous
commit: express the boiler plate details in the comment at the top of
the effect so that it can be auto-generated.

Part of that is that now the default values can be much more sanely
expressed: instead of setting the defaults as the particular integer
values the pot takes, express them in the user-visible units.

So the default noise gate level value can now be described as

    // POT: "Level" LINEAR(-100.0 -40.0) = -70.0 dB

instead of the inscrutable

    EFFECT_POT("Level", desc_dB, gate_pot0_level, 0),   // -70dB

where the default value of 0 ended up indeed being -70dB, but we had to
have a comment to that effect because it was so non-obvious (it came
from the fact that gate_pot0_level() did a linear interpolation between
-100 and -40, and -70 is the middle value).

So now the pot values make a lot more sense and defaults are easier to
see and set.

This also means that instead of having the pot values be -60 to +60 (in
order to make the default "noon" be zero and needing no initializer),
since we auto-generate the defaults we can make the actual internal
values be the more straightforward 0..120 range - not only matching what
we did for MIDI, but also simplifying a lot of the helper math cases.

As a result, the pot arrays are now done as 'unsigned char'.

While doing all this, I also noticed that the ->describe() function is
just entirely historical: it used to depend on the pot value for when
the enumerations were done as a separate hack.  But these days
enumeration pots are an integral part of the pot description, and the
->describe() functions were all just returning the unit string.

So get rid of the function pointer indirection, and just make it have a
simple and straightforward 'const char *unit' string.

This all makes the 'gen_effect' python script a bit bigger, but that is
more than made up for by the boiler plate removal in the effects
themselves, so not only does it make things clearer, this all removes
more lines than it adds.

And equally importantly, it means that now the Web UI actually can
convert the raw pot values into sensible units, because it too can take
the pot descriptions into account.  Some other minor UI updates while at
it.

All the python and JS scripting itself was obviously all done by AI.
Some day I might care enough to learn to actually write python, but for
now I'm perfectly happy just reading the end result.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Move all effects into 'effects/' subdirectory

.. leaving the audio helper headers in 'audio/'.

I'll make the auto-generation script pick up the effects list
automatically from the files in that directory, but I'll do that
separately: this is just the minimal file move.

Note that it's not enough to just enumerate the effects: the order of
effects also matters, so it's not quite as simple as just generating the
effect list from a simple directory listing.

So the next step is to add some more metadata to the effects files.

Right now the only "metadata" is the dummy wrapper macro just to mark
the pot descriptions.  I want to extend that too - it would be good to
actually contain the description and mapping of values too, so that
instead of using C function pointers the pot descriptions would have a
higher level abstraction that can be not only turned into the C code,
but also used for the Web MIDI side.

And the effect itself should have its own metadata - not just the
ordering requirement (as some kind of "priority number"), but the effect
name (and shortname) would be exposed too.

I'll have to think about it some more, but my rough plan would be to
have the metadata at the top of the effect file in a comment block that
is trivially parsed, and instead of having 'gen_effects.py' just
generate the trivial

   #include "../effects/{base}.h"

thing for effect_map.h, it would generate all the boiler plate for pot
values translations and all of 'struct effect' for that effect.

Make all the metadata simple enough that it can be easily translated
into both the actual C code running on the microcontroller, but also the
JS code running in the web app so that the Web MIDI UI shows proper pot
value ranges etc.

The above is a bit handwavy - I'll have to experiment.  But my thinking
would be that the gate effect - just to pick a random example - would go
from having pot functions and a 'struct effect' like this:

    static float gate_pot0_level(signed char pot)
    {
        // -100dB .. -40dB is 0.01mV..10mV peak signal level
        // If your noise floor is anywhere near -100dB, you don't need the
        // gate in the first place, but maybe it's a good way to actually
        // _see_ what your noise floor is...
        return linear_pot(pot, -100.0f, -40.0f);
    }
    [...]
    static struct effect gate_effect = {
        .name = "Noise Gate",
        .short_name = "GATE",
        .init = gate_init,
        .step = gate_step,
        .pots = {
            EFFECT_POT("Level", desc_dB, gate_pot0_level, 0),       // -70dB
            EFFECT_POT("Attack", desc_ms, gate_pot1_attack, -42),   // ~1.5ms
            EFFECT_POT("Release", desc_ms, gate_pot2_release, -30), // ~150ms
        }
    };

to having a comment header at the top of the effect:

    // NAME: Noise Gate [GATE]
    // PRIORITY: 1
    //    POT: "Level" LINEAR(-100 -40) dB
    //    POT: "Attack" LINEAR(0 10) ms
    //    POT: "Release" LINEAR(50 500) ms

and gen_effects.py would just generate the boilerplate code for the
interfaces, while the actual real meat of the effect (the init and step
functions) would remain as-is.

As always, the EQ effect is special, because it does that whole graph
thing.  So we'd have to have a special case for that, but that would
probably be just a simple

    //    GRAPH: eq_graph

at least for now, and only graphing the frequency response on the pedal,
not in the Web UI thing.

Anyway - that's the plan.  But for now, just separate out the effects
headers from the other code.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add Web app for MIDI state changes

This was largely because I wanted to test the whole MIDI thing without
always having to build a separate "host" and "device" pedal and checking
that they speak to each other.

Instead, I can just keep the device pedal connected to the computer both
for programming and for testing (well, at least for testing the regular
device side).

And initially I thought I'd do some local thing using libusb (not my
favorite thing ever, but I've used it for the dive computer side so at
least I'm familiar with it), but since I also need a UI...

So instead I decided that "hey, maybe I would just want to do it on a
phone with USB OTG and ask AI to generate some Web app"

Because let's face it.  I'm no good at UI's.  Or JavaScript.  A toddler
on crack would do a better job at it than I do at either of those.

It's not actually running on my phone - yet - but I can test it on my
desktop, and it should be fairly straightforward to just turn it into a
phone web app too, but that's for later if this whole "use MIDI to
control the pedal" actually turns out to be a good idea.

It might all be me being crazy.  I actually have a Sonicake "Pocket
Control" MIDI controller together with an expression pedal that should
arrive today for testing.  Because I don't know if any of this is
actually even remotely right: it could be that I just have a buggy
guitar pedal that just happens to work together with a buggy Web app.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Make the MIDI control use the new pot mapping

.. and also make pot changes generate MIDI messages in USB device mode
too, not just in USB host mode.

That way you get bidirectional updates, so that the host can also see
the device pot changes.

And since the host would also want to see what the initial values are,
add a STATE_DUMP_CC MIDI message, so that when you connect the two
together they can synchronize from known state rather than having to
always start from scratch.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix USB device descriptor for the composite audio / MIDI device case

The USB device descriptor needs a "Interface Association Descriptor
(IAD)" for the MIDI part.  Add it.

Since the pedal exposes a composite interface of both the audio
interface (for audio in and out) and the MIDI interface (for controlling
the effects), it should have that interface association descriptor to
tell the other side that the two interfaces go together and control the
same function.

I don't think Linux actually cares, but Antigravity tells me apparently
Windows needs it to load the MIDI drivers, so let's do it right.

Of course, I have no way of testing whether this really makes any
difference.  But in my cunning plan to completely revolutionize the
whole audio market with my incredible guitar pedal, I will have to take
over the Windows market too.

 "The same thing we do every night, Pinky - try to take over the world!"

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Mark the pot descriptors so that we can easily auto-generate pot lists

This is part of the whole "control things over MIDI" thing, which needs
a list of pots that can be controlled.

While at it, make the 'effects[]' array be auto-generated too.  This
needs some more cleanup, right now it just effectively moves the list of
effects from audio/effect.h into the CMakeLists.txt file instead, which
isn't really much of an improvement, but I'll have to think more about
how I want to do this.

I *suspect* the answer is that I'll just split the 'audio' subdirectory
in two, and move the effects into a separate 'effect' subdirectory,
while leaving the "helper utility headers" in 'audio'.

But for now this is mainly just a minimal "mark the pot descriptors for
easy scripting" together with a script to generate some headers with
that information in them (including a 'effects.js' header for a Web UI).

... and since I still really don't do python - or Web UIs, for that
matter - that script was entirely by antigravity.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Merge https://github.com/clevelandmusicco/GuitarPedal

Merge effect updates from Ricky Sheaves.

This makes some of the effects quite a bit cheaper in memory and/or in
CPU use.  It enables flush-to-zero for denormals which can make a big
difference, uses a few less filters in the reverb, and makes the echo
effect use 16-bit integers for the delay path, saving a lot of memory.

I made the %fpscr register accesses use the compiler built-ins instead
of inline asm - it's not like I dislike the inline asm in general, but
in this case it seems simpler to just use the compiler infrastructure.

Also, Ricky added an isb instruction to flush the pipeline - that's one
of those "technically correct" things to do to synchronize the fpscr
access, but it really doesn't matter in this case.  Even if there were
FPU instructions in flight (and there aren't), we simply don't care that
deeply. So keep it simple and stupid.

* https://github.com/clevelandmusicco/GuitarPedal:
  Echo: replace float[65536] delay line with int16_t[32768]
  Enable hardware FTZ on both cores; drop `reverb_flush()`
  Reverb: revert to 8 comb filters and 4 Schroeder allpass filters

Change pot value range from -100..+100 to -60..+60

So "100" looks like a rounder number to a human, and that's obviously
why I picked that original range.

But the -100..+100 range does not map very well to MIDI, which sends
7-bit numbers in the 0..127 range.  I started out with -63..+63
originally, but that really doesn't work when some of the settings (like
the "octaves" for the pitch shifter) really want nice divisors.

So '60' it is, and in some ways it is actually a "rounder" number than
100, in that it divides nicely into even more cases than 100 does.

While 100 is natural in base-10, it is only divisible by combinations of
two and five.  In contrast 60 is divisible by combinations of two, three
and five, and so maps well to things like that octave setting.

I don't think the reduced range (201 steps down to "only" 121 steps) is
actually noticeable.  We'll see.  There's "high-res MIDI" that sends
values in two parts, but that seems overkill.

The slider UI was already limited to only displaying 128 values simply
due to the resolution of the display, so ...

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Switch USB HID protocol to use MIDI over USB instead

The HID protocol was a mistake - I blame the fact that I have all the
musical ability of a snail on drugs.  The obviously correct answer is to
use MIDI, so that we could use an actual standard interface both on a
computer and even using things like external stomp switches.

As always, the USB code is written by Antigravity.  I think that's the
proper distribution of roles: Ricky has been doing any actual _musical_
effects, I've been doing the hardware interfaces, and Antigravity deals
with the tinyusb integration.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Echo: replace float[65536] delay line with int16_t[32768]

The `float array[65536]` delay line was consuming 256 KB -- 59% of the
entire 434 KB bss -- leaving only 7.5 KB of headroom against the 520 KB
SRAM limit. With `copy_to_ram` in effect, text + bss share the same
pool. A 7.5 KB margin is far too uncomfortable.

`audio/util.h`:
- Add `__sample_array_write_s16` / `sample_array_write_s16`: writes a
  `[-1, 1]` float to an `int16_t` cell as `val * 32767`.
- Add `__sample_array_read_s16` / `sample_array_read_s16`: converts two
  adjacent `int16_t` cells to float via `1/32767` and returns the
  linearly interpolated result. Same ring-buffer bitmask logic as the
  float variants.

`audio/echo.h`:
- `echo.array`: `float[65536]` (256 KB) -> `int16_t[32768]` (64 KB).
  Saves 192 KB. bss drops from 434 KB to 238 KB; SRAM headroom goes
  from 7.5 KB to ~199 KB. (!!!)
- `ECHO_DELAY_MAX_S`: 0.800 -> 0.672. The smaller array holds 32768
  samples at 48 kHz = 0.683 s. There's still plenty of margin for wow/flutter
  modulation. This tighter delay range is still in Maestro EP-1/2 territory.
- `ECHO_DELAY_LOG2_RATIO`: 4.0 -> 3.75 to match.
- `read_pos` clamp: 65534.0 -> 32766.0 to match the new buffer size.
- Read/write calls updated to `sample_array_read_s16` /
  `sample_array_write_s16`.
- And here's the controversial change:16-bit quantization noise sits at
~-96 dBFS (CD quality), below the guitar noise floor, and is further
attenuated by the playback LPF on every pass. We're emulating a tape
recorder from the 1960s, which had a dynamic range of ~65-75 dBFS.
This roughly maps to an 11 to 13-bit digital scale. So, arguably, it's much
more authentic now ;)
- Change default pot values:
  - `Time`: 46 -> 55 (~374.7 ms via the log taper).
  - `WowFlut`: 0 -> -50 (25% depth via `linear_pot`).

Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Enable hardware FTZ on both cores; drop `reverb_flush()`

`enable_ftz()` sets the FZ bit (24) in FPSCR via inline assembly on
both cores at startup. The Cortex-M33 VFPv5 FPU handles subnormals in
hardware rather than via a software trap, but still takes a 5-20x
penalty per operation. Any feedback path that decays to sub-1e-38 will
hit this without FTZ enabled, not just reverb's comb filters.

The old `reverb_flush()` only protected `filterstore` in the comb loop.
Hardware FTZ covers every float op in the chain: allpass buffers, echo
feedback, and any future effect, without per-site code needed.

FPSCR is per-core state, so `enable_ftz()` is called in both `main()`
and `audio_processing()`.

Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Reverb: revert to 8 comb filters and 4 Schroeder allpass filters

Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Use 'copy_to_ram' in order to avoid running out of flash

Now with a lot more effects, we started to lose samples when enabling
the more expensive ones.  And when I did some testing with unrolling
loops to improve code quality actually made it worse.

The actual performance issue ends up being that now that we have more
effects, we're also blowing out the XIP cache.  It's only 16kB in size,
and once you start missing in the XIP cache you get the whole hot of
waiting for flash.  Which really hurts on that simple in-order core.

Now, we don't have a ton of SRAM on the rp2354 either, and obviously
'copy_to_ram' will mean that now we have even less, when the boot phase
will copy the code into that precious resource.

But we have enough for the current effects, and with this simple
one-liner I can enable every single effect without any missing samples.

It's definitely getting to the point where I think any future effects
will have to start kicking out some less worthy existing ones.  The
pitch shifter is probably bound to be the first to go, even if I enjoy
how ridiculous it sounds.

We could try to be more granular, and only move the functions that run
as part of the audio loop on the second core into RAM, but I'm not sure
it's worth the effort compared to the one-liner build setting.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Merge https://github.com/clevelandmusicco/GuitarPedal

Pull new and updated effects from Ricky Sheaves:
 "This is fun. I spent hours today converting code from various
  projects.

  In addition to the effects you already have, these round out the
  'essentials' rather nicely, I think. These are 90% of everything
  I use on a weekly basis:

    Vibrato
	A must for organ-like tones (and full-blown chorus with the MIX at 50%)

    Reverb
	This one took some tuning given the CPU budget and the growing FX chain

    Preamp
	Tube / JFET saturation (different than Boost)

    Tremolo
	Standard issue; I added the somewhat-rare harmonic mode

    Echo
	No big changes, but I had to tune it once Reverb + Echo couldn't
	play nicely

  The commit messages pretty much cover it all"

Note that the reverb effect in particular is fairly expensive, and it's
easy to overwhelm the poor little RP2354 when enabling lots of effects.

The UI will not keep you from overwhelming the MCU, but you'll notice
it: the sound turns scratchy and bad, and the right-hand LED will grow
more brightly to show signal problems.

[ The right-hand LED also glows brightly for signal clipping, but it's
  typically pretty easy to tell whether it glowing due to clipping or
  due to a sample loss due to a overwhelmed CPU.

  They sound very different - a rather "scratchy" sound when missing
  samples vs a loud distorted signal. And their behavior pattern is
  different too: the clipping obviously happens with loud signals and
  tends to be temporary, while the overwhelmed CPU tends to be a pretty
  constant thing depending purely on the number (and type) of effects
  enabled, not the amplitude of the output ]

* https://github.com/clevelandmusicco/GuitarPedal:
  Tremolo: fix the harmonic tremolo level drop
  Add tremolo effect with NORM and HARM modes
  Reduce reverb CPU load; minor echo optimisations
  Reverb: expand to 12 combs/6 allpasses, add per-comb LFO modulation
  Add Freeverb reverb effect (Schroeder-Moorer, mono 48 kHz)
  Add preamp and vibrato effects
  Tape Echo: remove cruft and tweak performance

eeprom: only use 16 bytes per effect save area

I originally reserved 32 bytes per effect for saving to the eeprom, with
the idea that I'd have a secondary save area and only a fairly small
number of effects.  Except I never did that secondary save area, and the
effects have kept growing.

Since I just picked the simplest 2kbit i2c eeprom there is, the whole
save area is just 256 bytes in size.  That makes the i2c programming
very simple, but it meant that with 32 bytes per effect it could only
save 8 effects.

We already have more than that (counting the USB "effect"), and Ricky
has been doing a few more.  So let's just get rid of the theoretical
secondary save area, and give each effect just 16 bytes of eeprom.

While doing that, I'm also updating the checksum to cover more of the
effect data, so that when you change an effect (rename it, or to add new
state or whatever), there's a higher likelihood that the checksum won't
match some random old setting, and the state will instead reset to
defaults rather than something nonsensical.

The checksum literally exists just for that "I re-orderd the effects or
changed the pot meanings of the pots, and it should reset to something
sane instead of becoming something senseless".  So let's make it better
for that.

[ Also change the default for the pitch effect to be one octave up,
  since that's the silly setting it was "designed" for ]

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add USB host/device mode build options

This adds the option for the USB-C connector to be used as a way to
communicate the UI state between two pedals over USB HID.

The default setting is that the pedal is a USB device that exposes both
USB audio interfaces and a USB HID interface.

The other configuration is to build the "UI pedal" as a USB host: no
audio capabilities, but it can communicate over the USB HID interface
with the audio pedal, and it has the screen and the controls on it.

It also means that when you connect the audio box to a computer, not
only do you get the audio interface, the new USB HID interface could be
used to change all the effect settings dynamically from the computer
too.

It's currently a specialized magic HID interface that is very closely
tied to the particular effects versions on the pedal, so it's not very
convenient as a control interface, but that can hopefully be fixed
eventually with a slightly more thought out interface.

There could be variations on this model, where the audio box has
possibly a single on-off stomp switch and maybe a master volume knob, so
it doesn't have to be entirely hardcoded.  But since the audio pedal
does have the EEPROM with effect settings, it would be entirely useful
on its own even without the UI connected.

The UI pedal could also possibly talk MIDI, and thus extend on the UI
that way.

This is all very hand-wavy and experimental.  I don't have such hardware
yet, but I can test this by just connecting two of the existing pedals,
with one acting as the audio pedal and the other as the UI pedal.

It is unclear if any actual user would want to do it this way, although
Ricky Sheaves did point me at pedals like the Orange OMEC Teleport that
he has.  That works as a limited version of my envisioned audio pedal -
just without the built-in effects.

I'm doing this because I want to play with form factors once more, and
separating the audio side from the UI means that I can play with one
without having to worry about the other.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Tremolo: fix the harmonic tremolo level drop

The old HARM formula was:

    lo*(1 + k*lfo) + hi*(1 - k*lfo)  ==  (lo+hi) + k*lfo*(lo-hi)

The two filters (LP at 144.7 Hz, HP at 636.6 Hz) are not a
complementary crossover pair, so `lo+hi` has a broad mid-frequency
dip around 8 dB at 300 Hz. That made HARM noticeably quieter
than NORM at the same gain staging.

New formula:

    in + k*lfo*(lo - hi)

The modulation term `k*lfo*(lo-hi)` is identical; only the carrier
changes from `lo+hi` to `in`.

- Unity gain at zero depth, matching NORM behaviour.
- At mid frequencies the apparent depth per unit `k` is reduced. Increasing the depth control compensates.
- At frequency extremes one branch dominates and depth is unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Add tremolo effect with NORM and HARM modes

Just three controls.

RATE: 0.1-10 Hz, cubic
DEPTH
MODE (NORM/HARM).

NORM mode uses bipolar AM: gain = 1 + k*lfo, where k = depth/(2-depth).
Average level stays at 1.0 at all depth settings, so 100% depth swings
0..2x rather than cutting average level by up to 6 dB.

HARM mode models the Fender 6G4 harmonic vibrato circuit with two
one-pole filters: a LP at 144.7 Hz (220k/5nF) for the low branch and a
HP at 636.6 Hz (1M/250pF, computed as in-LP) for the high branch. The
LFO modulates them in opposite phase. The two corners are not
complementary, so there is a broad mid-frequency dip and phasey
recombination on summing, which is what gives the brownface character.

Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Reduce reverb CPU load; minor echo optimisations

While testing, I discovered that loading reverb and echo at the same
time resulted in audio artefacts. I don't have a profiler or cycle
counter on the hardware, so I made these changes a couple at a time
until the noise/distortion/crackle disappeared from the combined
echo loop + reverb tail. Not very scientific, and my math may not be
close to right, but it worked.

Reverb:
- Drop from 12 to 10 parallel FBCFs; scale `REVERB_FIXEDGAIN` up from
  0.007 to 0.0084 to preserve wet level with fewer combs; reverb still
  sounds OK
- Remove fractional-delay interpolation from the comb read: one buffer
  load per comb instead of two, dropping the lerp multiply-adds
- Eliminate the redundant `depth` clamp in the comb loop -- all ten
  delay values (1215-1907) leave more than `REVERB_MOD_DEPTH` (6)
  samples of headroom, so the branch was always taken; inline the
  constant directly
- Remove `reverb_flush` from the allpass chain; the 0.5 feedback
  coefficient guarantees decay, so subnormals cannot accumulate there

Echo:
- Precompute `tanhf(preamp_asymmetry)` once in `echo_init` as
  `preamp_dc_offset`; the value is constant but `tanhf` is not
  folded by the compiler from a `const` struct field
- Cache equal-power blend gains (`dry_gain`, `wet_gain`); recompute
  `fastsincos` only when `blend` drifts more than 0.001, matching the
  existing `last_tone` guard pattern for the playback LPF

Rough cycles/sample saved (M33 @ 172.8 MHz, 3600 cycles/sample budget):

```
| Change                                               | ~cycles/sample |
|------------------------------------------------------|----------------|
| 12 -> 10 combs (2 full comb iterations eliminated)   |             60 |
| Remove lerp from comb read (2 loads -> 1)            |             70 |
| Remove redundant `depth` clamp in comb loop          |             35 |
| Remove `reverb_flush` from 6 allpasses               |             18 |
| Precompute `tanhf(preamp_asymmetry)` in `echo_init`  |             50 |
| Cache blend `fastsincos` (saved on ~99.9% of samples)|             12 |
| **Total**                                            |       **~245** |
```

I say "rough" becuase is really just an instruction count and that't it.
But, ~7% of the per-sample budget. Lerp removal and comb count reduction
are the bulk of it. The `tanhf` saving is disproportionate for one line: it
goes through `exp` internally (~50 cycles on M33). Comb buffer
reads are non-sequential loads, so real savings may be somewhat less
than the instruction count suggests.

NOTE: if we enable flush-to-zero by default on the MP33 FPU, we could save
up to ~40 cycles/sample in addition to the stuff above. Might be as simple
as

  // FPU context is per-core; must be set on core 1 separately.
  __set_FPSCR(__get_FPSCR() | 0x01000000); // FZ bit (bit 24)

at the top of `audio_processing()`. I'll leave that for Linus to suss out, though.

Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Reverb: expand to 12 combs/6 allpasses, add per-comb LFO modulation

Standard Freeverb produces metallic ringing in long tails because fixed
integer delays create sharp resonant peaks. Extending the filter bank
and adding LFO modulation on each comb read pointer breaks up the
periodicity.

DSP changes:
- Comb count 8 -> 12: four additional delay lengths continuing the
  original spacing pattern (1831, 1907, 1979, 2045 samples), all
  within the existing `REVERB_COMB_SIZE = 2048` buffer
- Allpass count 4 -> 6: two additional delays (153, 87 samples)
  continuing the descending sequence
- Four quadrature-phasor LFOs modulate each comb's read pointer:
  complex-multiply rotation per sample, no `sincos` in the hot path;
  rates 0.21/0.31/0.46/0.67 Hz (~3:2 geometric spacing to prevent
  beating); phases staggered 0/0.25/0.5/0.75 cycles at init
- Comb read upgraded from integer to linearly-interpolated fractional
  delay; modulation depth clamped to `min(6 samples, buffer headroom)`
  so the read pointer can never lap the write pointer
- LFOs assigned round-robin to the 12 combs (`i % 4`)

Gain constants retuned for the larger filter bank:
- `fixedgain` 0.015 -> 0.010 (proportional scaling for 12 combs)
- `scalewet` 3.0 -> 1.5, `scaledry` 2.0 -> 1.2 (unity dry at 0% wet)
- Damp range [0.0, 0.4] -> [0.1, 0.5]: fully undamped tails are
  rarely useful and the old low end was dead space on the pot
- Default Mix -50 -> -65 (0.175 wet), Damp 0 -> 15 (pole = 0.33)

Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Add Freeverb reverb effect (Schroeder-Moorer, mono 48 kHz)

Jezar's public-domain Freeverb algorithm, ported to the pedal's
sample-at-a-time mono path at 48 kHz.

DSP topology:
- 8 parallel feedback comb filters (FBCF), all fed directly from
  the input; each has a one-pole LP in its feedback path
- 4 series Schroeder allpass filters on the summed comb output
- Delay lengths are the canonical Freeverb 44100 Hz values scaled
  to 48000 Hz (multiply by 48/44.1)

Parameters:
- Mix: linear dry/wet, with `fixedgain` (0.015) on the comb input
  and `scalewet`/`scaledry` (3.0/2.0) normalising levels
- Room: feedback gain `g` in [0.70, 0.98] via roomscale/roomoffset
- Damp: one-pole LP pole in [0, 0.4]; higher = more HF rolloff in
  the FBCF feedback path

Two hardware workarounds required:
- `reverb_flush()` manually zeros subnormals in the comb and allpass
  buffers; the Cortex-M33 FPU does not flush-to-zero by default,
  causing ~100x slowdown once the reverb tail decays below 1e-38
- All `reverb_state` fields including `.delay` are set in
  `reverb_init()` because pico-sdk silently zeroes large static  objects
during the .data copy from flash

Registered in `effects[]` between echo and pitch.

Add preamp and vibrato effects

**Preamp** (`preamp.h`)

Wait, don't we already have a Boost effect? Yes, but ...

The current boost effect does wavefolding: it hard-clips by reflecting the
signal back on itself, generating mostly odd-order harmonics with a sharp
transition at the clip boundary. That's perfect for aggressive clipping or
distortion pedal simulation, but it is not how a class-A analog front end
behaves.

Preamp uses asymmetrically biased tanh saturation. Biasing the waveshaper
off-centre generates even-order harmonics (mostly 2nd), which is the magick
behind the warm character of class-A tube and JFET stages. The distortion onset
is gradual; there is no clip boundary; just a soft knee. So, at moderate drive
settings the signal is more coloured than clipped. Players who want 'always-on'
front-end character rather than an obvious clipping stage tend to prefer this.

Usage: select Voice (Tube or JFET), dial Sat from 0.5x (clean) to 4x (hard
clip), trim Level +/-20 dB. Works best early in the chain, typically first.

- Tube voice models two cascaded 12AX7 triode stages using `tanhf()` as the
waveshaper. A fixed 0.15 grid-bias offset on each stage pushes the operating
point off-centre, generating even-order harmonics for vintage-amp character.
- An interstage DC block (~38 Hz, one-pole IIR) strips the stage-1 DC offset
before stage 2 so the asymmetry doesn't accumulate.
- JFET voice models a single common-emitter 2N5457-like stage with three
frequency-domain features: an emitter-bypass low shelf (~120 Hz, -6 dB), an
asymmetric `tanhf()` waveshaper with a 0.12 bias offset, and a Miller-cap HF
rolloff (~9 kHz one-pole LPF).
- Output normalization constants (`PREAMP_TUBE_NORM`, `PREAMP_JFET_NORM`) are
precomputed at the default drive of 1.2x so unity gain is preserved (well, just
barely above, actually) at the default settings.

**Vibrato** (`vibrato.h`)

Usage: set Rate (0.1-8 Hz) for LFO speed, Depth (0-5 ms) for pitch swing, Mix
for dry/wet balance. At 100% wet you get pure pitch vibrato; blend in dry signal
for chorus. 100% dry with a Rate of ~5 Hz makes for a nice rotary speaker
emulation.

- Writes incoming samples into a 1024-entry ring buffer (~21 ms at 48 kHz) and
reads back with a fractionally interpolated index offset by a sine LFO riding on
a 6 ms center delay.
- The center delay keeps the read head from overtaking the write head even at
maximum depth (6 ms + 5 ms = 11 ms, well inside the 21 ms buffer).
- Mix uses an equal-power crossfade: `dry = cos(0.25 * mix)`, `wet = sin(0.25 *
mix)`, computed once in `vibrato_init` via `fastsincos`.

**effect.h**

- Add `desc_s()` unit descriptor (seconds) alongside the existing Hz/ms/dB
helpers (will be used by a future reverb effect).
- Insert `#include "preamp.h"` and `EFF(preamp)` immediately after `gate` (new
index 1).
- Insert `#include "vibrato.h"` and `EFF(vibrato)` immediately after `flanger`
(new index 6).
- **Note:** inserting effects mid-array shifts all subsequent effect indices,
which shifts their EEPROM page addresses. You'll need to hold both encoders down
with no USB connection to reset after first boot.
